entries.title: Davis Martin caught tipping pitches in Red Sox' pounding of White Sox
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON — White Sox starter Davis Martin thought something was up by the comfortable swings the Red Sox were taking during their six-run first inning Tuesday.</p><p>“Some of the adjustments we made there after, we started getting a lot more weak contact, a lot more swing and miss,” Martin said. “I definitely think there’s something to it. So something we have to go look at in between starts and see if we can clean it up.”</p><p>That something is tipping. If it seemed like the Red Sox knew what was coming early in their 14-2 pounding of the White Sox, it’s probably because they did. In that fateful first, the Red Sox hit two singles, a double and two home runs, including a grand slam by Caleb Durbin.</p><p>“We’re going to go back and see what the tip is and how long we’ve been doing it and if that’s going to answer some questions,” said Martin, who allowed nine earned runs in the game and has given up 23 in his last 25 ⅔ innings, covering five starts. “If it doesn’t, we still have to make some better pitches. But it would explain some things.”</p><p>Injured catcher Kyle Teel caught the tipping from the dugout and alerted Martin and new catcher Joey Bart.</p><p>“It just seemed like every wrinkle we threw at them they capitalized [on],” Bart said. “A lot of times you get away with a lot of stuff, and tonight we didn’t. The Red Sox have a history of being really good with that. You know that going into the series. They’ve always been on top of that. So credit to them; it’s part of the game.”</p><p>Erick Fedde, in his first outing since moving to the bullpen, followed Martin and didn’t fare much better, allowing four runs (three earned) in the Red Sox’ second six-run inning of the game in the sixth. The Red Sox, who have 24 victories in their last 27 games, showed no signs of slowing down and no mercy. The 14 runs tied for the most the White Sox have allowed this year.</p><p>The White Sox’ hitters weren’t much better than their pitchers, though they equaled their run total (two) from the series in which the Red Sox swept them last month at Rate Field. At least the White Sox won’t face two of the pitchers who stymied them in that series, lefties Payton Tolle and Jake Bennett. But on Wednesday they get Sonny Gray, who’s 13-2 with a 2.93 ERA.</p><h3>Questions with Quero</h3><p>White Sox manager Will Venable shared some behind-the-scenes insight into catcher Edgar Quero’s demotion to Triple-A Charlotte. Though Quero came on at the plate in the last week, he still wasn’t doing enough to keep his spot.</p><p>“The things that we’ve asked him to do in the weight room, the training room, some of the preparation stuff, he’s really done a nice job of that, and we saw positive results from that,” Venable said. “But we really believe strongly that there’s even more of a better version of him out there, and to send him back down to work on those things I think is really important.”</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>In addition to Quero, the Sox optioned left-hander Tyler Schweitzer to Charlotte. He had posted back-to-back outings of three scoreless innings in relief. The Sox also activated lefty Tyler Gilbert from the injured list and optioned him to Charlotte.</p><p>• Rehabbing outfielder Austin Hays (strained left calf) has seven hits in his last 23 at-bats for Charlotte, including three homers. But general manager Chris Getz said the Sox don’t have clarity on his status. “It’s been a long road for him,” Getz said. “We have decisions ahead of us.”</p><p>• Shortstop Roch Cholowsky, whom the Sox selected with the first pick in the MLB Draft, made his professional debut at High-A Winston-Salem. entries.title: Homer Glen neighborhood ordered to shelter in place due to barricaded home invasion suspect
entries.summary: <p>A shelter in place order was in effect for a Homer Glen neighborhood Tuesday evening after a home invasion suspect barricaded themselves, according to Darien police.</p><p>Officers were still "working to take the suspect into custody" at 10 p.m. Tuesday, according to Darien police. Residents on the street were ordered to shelter in place, and Maverick Trail was closed at Woodland and Parker, the Will County Sheriff's office said on social media.</p><p>Officers responded to the 1400 block of Sequoia Drive shortly after 2 p.m. for a report of a home invasion and saw a suspect flee in a vehicle, police said. They chased him to the Bell Road and 143rd Street in Homer Glen, where he barricaded himself into a residence.</p><p>One victim was hospitalized with "non-life threatening injuries" and has since been released, police said.</p>

entries.title: New White Sox Brenton Doyle, Joey Bart noticed team having fun from afar
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON — The White Sox have caught the attention of players around the major leagues, and it’s not just because they’re vastly exceeding expectations.</p><p>It’s because they’re having a ball doing it.</p><p>“It’s hard to miss,” new center fielder Brenton Doyle said Tuesday, “whether it’s the wizardry going on or just everyone always having a blast in the dugout — big smiles, a lot of energy. I think that goes a long way, especially in this sport. You got to keep good vibes throughout the whole year.”</p><p>Doyle was one of two players the White Sox acquired before the trade deadline Monday, along with catcher Joey Bart, who started in their first game with their new team Tuesday against the surging Red Sox. Doyle is excited to join the party.</p><p>“I admired it from afar and always thought they were having so much fun out there,” said Doyle, who came from the Rockies, with whom he won two Gold Gloves (2023-24). “The energy was off the charts.”</p><p>Bart, who came from the Braves after starting the season with the Pirates, also noticed the Sox’ vibe, but in a different way.</p><p>“Seeing Mike Vasil on ‘SportsCenter’ every night,” Bart said of the White Sox’ wizard in chief. “I got to know him in the offseason. He’s a great dude. Just seems like a lot of fun energy. Seems like guys are playing pretty loose. Usually that’s how you end being good.”</p><p>With the Red Sox starting left-hander Patrick Sandoval, manager Will Venable put both right-handed-hitting Bart and Doyle in the lineup. He said that’s how he’ll use Doyle, who will platoon with Tristan Peters in center. Bart and Drew Romo will split time behind the plate.</p><p>Edgar Quero was the odd man out at catcher, demoted to Triple-A Charlotte despite a recent run of success at the plate. He had five hits in his last 14 at-bats, including a walk-off single to beat the Yankees. But the Sox preferred keeping Romo and adding Bart.</p><p>“That was a tough decision,” Venable said. “He made it tougher than the last time we had to make the same decision. There’s two parts to the decision: One is Romo behind the plate, the X-factor qualities that he brings; also the objective things defensively that he brings we really like, we’ve been benefitting from.”</p><p>Bart has the challenge of learning his third pitching staff this season. He told Venable he was on his computer studying up on the White Sox’ staff soon after being traded.</p><p>“It takes some time to build relationships with everybody,” Bart said. “It’s something I’ve done before. I’ve done it a couple times now. Just using the resources, talking to everybody. Trying to figure out what makes them go. The sooner we can bridge that gap, the better. But it does always take a little bit of time.”</p><p>Doyle is healthy again after missing two months with an oblique injury that frustrated him because he went three consecutive seasons without going on the injury list.</p><p>“Really dynamic athlete, is as fast as anybody in the league,” Venable said. “Plus defender; a guy that had to cover a lot of ground in center field at Coors Field. And on days he’s not playing, to have those types of legs on the bench, a guy who can come in and steal a bag, do some things on the bases and defensively, as well, is going to be a nice thing to have for us.”</p><p>What’s nice for Doyle after enduring three consecutive 100-loss seasons with the Rockies is a shot at the playoffs — much like it is for Sox fans.</p><p>“It’s huge,” Doyle said. “I’ve never really come close to being part of playoff baseball. I’m really looking forward to the opportunity, and I’m thankful for the White Sox to give it to me.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Man charged in separate murders of woman, teen girl on East Side
entries.summary: <p>A 21-year-old man has been charged with fatally shooting two teen girls in separate incidents on the East Side dating back to 2024, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Anthony Nunnally faces two counts of first-degree murder in the killings of Gabriella Arellano, 17, and Sierra Evans, 19, police announced Tuesday.</p><p>Arellano <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/10/26/woman-shot-east-side" target="_blank" ><u>was found</u></a> shot twice in the head in the 11000 block of South Mackinaw Avenue on Oct. 26, 2025, according to police.</p><p>Evans <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2024/09/28/woman-found-shot-to-death-on-far-south-side" target="_blank" ><u>was found</u></a> outside with gunshot wounds in the 9500 block of South Avenue N on Sept. 28, 2024, police said.</p><p>Nunnally was due in court Wednesday, police said.</p>

entries.title: Cubs get first crack at Dodgers' Tarik Skubal, but will there be another one in October?
entries.summary: <p>On one side of the Great Dodgers-<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> Gap now stands Tarik Skubal, the best left-handed pitcher on the planet, maybe the finest hurler of ’em all.</p><p>Skubal, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-dodgers-tarik-skubal-tigers-jed-hoyer-trades-brewers-nl-playoffs-kevin-gausman-matt-shaw-injury" target="_blank" >grand prize of baseball’s trade deadline</a>, was on the mound — and lost — Tuesday at Wrigley Field for the two-time-defending world champions, a colossus of an organization that takes whatever it wants, destroys everything in its path, spends insatiably on its roster and seemingly exists for the sole purpose of winning the final game of each and every season.</p><p>“The entire focus of this organization is on winning championships,” Skubal told reporters after arriving at Wrigley for a three-game series against a Cubs team the Dodgers could see again in October.</p><p>After scoring twice off Skubal in a 5-1 win, the Cubs can hope to get another crack at Skubal in a Game 1 at Dodger Stadium when that time comes. Not that facing the 2024 and 2025 American League Cy Young winner is ever a picnic.</p><p>Cubs fans booed Skubal as he stretched in right field before the game, and again as he emerged from the bullpen and walked to the dugout. History will show his first batter faced in Dodger blue was one of baseball’s biggest stars, Pete Crow-Armstrong, who watched strike three — a 99-mph sinker — blow by. It will also show Skubal went six good innings, though Dansby Swanson dinged him for a solo homer and Nico Hoerner added a two-out, run-scoring infield hit. Skubal left with the Cubs ahead 2-1.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">dansby left no doubt about that one. <a href="https://t.co/31VULxP4vH">pic.twitter.com/31VULxP4vH</a></p>— Chicago Cubs (@Cubs) <a href="https://x.com/Cubs/status/2084803204743647292?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 5, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Is Skubal the missing piece the Dodgers needed to make it three titles in a row? No, they already had more than enough to pull it off without him. But now they might go into the postseason as one of the heaviest favorites ever.</p><p>And barring the unforeseeable, Skubal will be the Game 1 starter in a rotation that could be so strong come playoff time, it’s almost mind-boggling to contemplate. While other teams, including the Cubs, will hope to have three or four legitimately worthy arms to start the most important games of the season, the Dodgers — if healthy — will have to choose among Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Shohei Ohtani, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow and Roki Sasaki, not to mention current 11-game winner Justin Wroblewski.</p><p>“I’m not going to sit here and say I’m the big piece,” Skubal said. “They’ve been a pretty good team without me.”</p><p>The filthy rich get filthy richer, and so it goes.</p><p>In the wake of the trade deadline, there are many questions being asked in regard to the Dodgers’ unsurprising acquisition of Skubal, who is 29 and a pending free agent.</p><p>Why were they able to land him from the Tigers in exchange for a prospect package that doesn’t seem to have wowed anybody?</p><p>Why wasn’t this the occasion of all occasions for the soaring Brewers, with their elite farm system, to go for the jugular and better position themselves — imagine a 1-2 of Skubal and Jacob Misiorowski — to at last win a World Series?</p><p>Oh, and this one: Are the Dodgers ruining baseball? When the team that leads all others in annual revenue — $850 million in 2025, according to Forbes’ annual valuations — adds a Skubal-size piece to what already was a mountainous collection of talent and a monstrous payroll, it’s bound to add fuel to MLB owners’ arguments for addressing competitive imbalance with a salary cap. Some already are envisioning a line from the Skubal trade to a shutdown of the 2027 season.</p><p>But back to the Great Dodgers-Cubs Gap, which is as evident as ever.</p><p>Since the Cubs eliminated the Dodgers in the 2016 NLCS, the Dodgers have averaged over 100 wins per season and 17 more than the Cubs, a massive difference. The Dodgers are on pace to finish with a better record than the Cubs for the eighth straight season.</p><p>Yes, the Dodgers easily outspend the Cubs on players — a $700 million contract for Ohtani, $365 million for Mookie Betts, $325 million for Yamamoto, $240 million for Tucker, $162 million for Freddie Freeman, on and on, all of it staggering. But their outlay for payroll and luxury-tax penalties also equals a significantly higher percentage of their total revenue than the Cubs spend. Again, the Dodgers are all in it to win it in a way almost nobody else is.</p><p>It’s a heck of a gap, though the Cubs, after their own excellent trade deadline, do have hope of getting to the World Series themselves. After all, five 100-plus-win Dodgers teams in the last decade have failed to win it all.</p><p>“It’s our job and everyone else’s job to try to make [a Dodgers three-peat] not happen,” Cubs president of baseball operations Jed Hoyer said.</p><p>It’s going to require some kind of a heavy lift, that’s for sure.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" >Jed Hoyer gets aggressive at trade deadline, deals prospects with Cubs’ present in mind: ‘We’re here to win’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-dodgers-tarik-skubal-tigers-jed-hoyer-trades-brewers-nl-playoffs-kevin-gausman-matt-shaw-injury" >Cubs want to rule baseball world, but after trade deadline, they still need to get past juggernaut Dodgers</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-trade-deadline-clay-holmes-mets" target="_blank" >Cubs continue to bolster rotation, net Clay Holmes in swap with Mets</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Lefty struggles keep Ian Happ out of Cubs’ lineup as opportunity goes to trade-deadline get Tyrone Taylor
entries.summary: <p><b>Craig Counsell</b> wasn’t exactly harboring a secret about <b>Ian Happ</b>.</p><p>“Ian’s struggled against left-handed pitching this year, there’s no question,” the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ manager said before Tuesday’s game.</p><p>For a second straight night against a Dodgers southpaw starter, the Cubs’ left fielder did not start in left field, out of the lineup partially as a break during the team’s stretch of 17 games in 17 days – and partially as an acknowledgement that the team has better options at this moment in time.</p><p>Perhaps no lefty in the game is as formidable as the one the Dodgers threw Tuesday night, their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-dodgers-tarik-skubal-tigers-jed-hoyer-trades-brewers-nl-playoffs-kevin-gausman-matt-shaw-injury" >earth-shattering trade-deadline acquisition</a> <b>Tarik Skubal</b>.</p><p>It hasn’t mattered, though, whether the left-hander Happ’s gone up against has been a two-time Cy Young winner or not. He hasn’t hit them, coming into Tuesday with a .530 OPS against lefties – only eight of baseball’s qualified hitters started the day with a lower mark – versus his .820 number against righties.</p><p>Counsell didn’t make this sound like a permanent banishment for the All Star and Gold Glover, one of the mainstays in the Cubs’ lineup. But with outfielder <b>Tyrone Taylor</b> in on a trade-deadline deal with the Mets, there’s somewhere else to turn, for the moment, at least.</p><p>Team president <b>Jed Hoyer</b> revealed Monday that Taylor fulfilled what was on Counsell’s deadline wishlist: a right-handed hitter he could bring off the bench, something the Cubs were lacking with utility man <b>Matt Shaw</b> sidelined for the last month and a half with a hand sprain that refuses to go away.</p><p>Taylor arrived Tuesday with a .301 batting average and a .900 OPS in 77 plate appearances against lefties this season.</p><p>“Ian’s still going to play against some lefties,” Counsell said. “But Tyrone gives us somebody, he’s going to get at-bats against left-handed pitching, for sure, and we’ll just take it from there.”</p><p>A night earlier, <b>Kevin Alcantara</b> started in left field. He hit his first big league homer in the Cubs’ win over the Dodgers, was subbed out for Happ once the lefty starter exited and was sent to the minors upon Taylor’s arrival.</p><p>Might that be the playbook, at least in the immediate future? We’ll see. Given Happ’s track record, it’s possible one breakout performance against lefties could win back however much playing time he’s set to lose.</p><p>But for now, Tyrone Taylor, come on down.</p><p><b>Tough on Tucker</b></p><p>Fans let former Cubs outfielder <b>Kyle Tucker</b> know how they felt about his decision to ink a big-money free-agent deal with the juggernaut Dodgers, booing the outfielder at every turn during the first two games of a three-game series this week at Wrigley Field.</p><p>The Cubs acquired Tucker in a trade two offseasons ago, and he made the NL All-Star team after a spectacular first half last season. He was injured and slumped during the second half before leaving for free agency and $240 million from the back-to-back champs.</p><p>Whether Cubs fans felt spurned or just booed someone who joined baseball’s best team – Skubal, for example, received a similar treatment – they let Tucker have it.</p><p>Then Tucker let them have it, homering off <b>Javier Assad</b> in the second inning Tuesday.</p><p><b>Comeback trail</b></p><p>A trio of injured Cubs pitchers – lefty reliever <b>Hoby Milner</b>, righty starter <b>Edward Cabrera</b> and righty closer <b>Daniel Palencia</b> – are making their way back with minor league rehab appearances set for Wednesday with Triple-A Iowa.</p><p><b>New bullpen arm</b></p><p>The Cubs added righty reliever <b>Ryan Zeferjahn</b> to the active roster Tuesday after acquiring him in a deadline deal Monday, designating righty <b>Jake Woodford</b> for assignment to make room.</p>

entries.title: 16-year-old e-scooter rider fatally struck by driver in North Center
entries.summary: <p>A 16-year-old boy riding an e-scooter was fatally struck by a truck driver in North Center on Monday, the third teenager to be killed in traffic on e-scooters this year.</p><p>The teen was riding the scooter northbound in the 4100 block of North Western Avenue around 3:35 p.m. when he lost control and was hit by a semi-truck, Chicago police said in a statement. He was taken to Illinois Masonic Hospital, where he was pronounced dead, police said.</p><p>Citations were pending, and an investigation was ongoing, police said.</p><p>The boy, Alex Blacio, had been riding home from work, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/ayuda-para-funeral-de-alex" target="_blank" >GoFundMe</a> for the boy’s family.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DV1_3RQCtqu/" target="_blank" ></a></p><p>Scooter-related <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2024/10/09/lime-divvy-chicago-e-scooter-riders-serious-injuries" target="_blank" ><u>crashes have increased</u></a> alongside rising ridership over the past few years, prompting a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/05/04/chicago-launches-e-scooter-safety-campaign-in-wake-of-recent-scooter-deaths" target="_blank" ><u>safety</u></a> campaign from the city. The Chicago Fire Department responded to nearly 200 e-scooter-related incidents in 2022. That number had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/06/05/scooter-escooters-lane-tech-safety-teenagers-crashes" target="_blank" ><u>more than tripled by 2025</u></a>.</p><p>E-scooters have grown increasingly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/06/05/scooter-escooters-lane-tech-safety-teenagers-crashes" target="_blank" ><u>popular among students of Lane Tech College Prep</u></a>, less than a mile south from where the crash occurred.</p><p>So far this year, two other teens have been fatally struck by drivers while riding e-scooters: 17-year-old <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/05/01/loved-ones-launch-fundraiser-for-venezuelan-teenager-killed-in-south-side-scooter-crash" target="_blank" ><u>Astrid Alexandra Carrillo Noguera</u></a> and 15-year-old <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/22/girl-15-killed-while-riding-scooter-in-south-shore-hit-and-run" target="_blank" ><u>Violet Harris</u></a> were both killed in accidents on the South Side nearly a month apart this spring.</p><p>Six people on scooters or bikes were <a class="Link" href="https://api.chicago.gov/filenet5/servlets/getDocumentContent?applicationId=CompleteStreets&documentId=%7B601CB99F-0000-C917-A80A-59C827820B0F%7D" target="_blank" ><u>hit and killed by cars</u></a> between January and June of this year, compared to one in the same span last year. The number of traffic deaths — which the city had vowed to eliminate by this year — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/08/25/vision-zero-traffic-crash-deaths-pedestrian-cyclist-car-roads-streets" target="_blank" ><u>remains largely where it was 10 years ago</u></a> after a brief pandemic increase.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/06/05/scooter-escooters-lane-tech-safety-teenagers-crashes" >For Chicago teens, e-scooters are fun, convenient but sometimes dangerous, even deadly</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/05/04/chicago-launches-e-scooter-safety-campaign-in-wake-of-recent-scooter-deaths" >Chicago launches e-scooter safety campaign after recent deaths</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/08/25/vision-zero-traffic-crash-deaths-pedestrian-cyclist-car-roads-streets" >A decade ago, the city committed to eliminating traffic deaths by 2026. entries.title: Dodgers' three-peat? Cubs showcasing they can mount championship challenge: ‘That’s how this team is wired’
entries.summary: <p>It might seem as though the Death Star is fully operational after two-time Cy Young Award-winning left-hander <b>Tarik Skubal</b> was added to the most talent-rich team in baseball.</p><p>Is a Dodgers three-peat truly inevitable?</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a>, trailing in their own division, aren’t expected to enter October as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-dodgers-tarik-skubal-tigers-jed-hoyer-trades-brewers-nl-playoffs-kevin-gausman-matt-shaw-injury" target="_blank" >the sort of World Series favorites the Dodgers are</a>. But on back-to-back nights at an electrified Wrigley Field, they showed they have the ability to mount a challenge to the juggernaut.</p><p>After a 10-5 victory Monday, the Cubs were 5-1 winners Tuesday, besting the Dodgers and spoiling Skubal’s first outing for his new team.</p><p>‘‘That’s kind of just who we are,’’ shortstop <b>Dansby Swanson</b> said. ‘‘That’s how this team is built. That’s how this team is wired and really what we expect out of ourselves — to be able to play complete games, whether it’s on the bases, in the field, on the mound, in the batter’s box. There’s so many ways to be good at this game, and we take pride in being able to do all of it.</p><p>‘‘We’ve showcased that a lot of the year but especially over these last couple of days.’’</p><p>Swanson smashed a tying home run against Skubal in the third inning, the loudest of the two runs the Cubs scored against him. <b>Nico Hoerner’s</b> high chopper in the sixth broke a 1-all tie, and the Cubs scored a trio of insurance runs after Skubal’s exit.</p><p>More impressively, perhaps, the Cubs managed to outpitch Skubal and the Dodgers, with right-hander <b>Javier Assad</b> turning in his latest stellar effort and the bullpen pitching 3⅓ perfect innings.</p><p>Throw in a critical stolen base by <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> and a second highlight-reel defensive play in as many nights by <b>Pedro Ramirez</b>, and it was another all-around performance, the type of game these Cubs were built to play and one that could make them a true championship challenger to the dynasty-seeking Dodgers.</p><p>‘‘They play the game the right way,’’ newly acquired reliever <b>Ryan Zeferjahn</b> said of his new team. ‘‘They do every little thing right.’’</p><p>It’s only early August, but there was a distinct ‘‘October preview’’ vibe on the North Side.</p><p>‘‘I don’t want to say, ‘This is why we play,’ but come on,’’ Swanson said. ‘‘It’s kind of what you dream about as a kid: two of the better teams in the league . . . being able to go compete against each other in this atmosphere and environment, nighttime at Wrigley with a ton of fans.</p><p>‘‘That’s like the thing you do in the backyard when you’re a kid.’’</p><h3>Happ sits again</h3><p>Left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b> was out of the Cubs’ starting lineup for a second consecutive night against a left-handed starter, with manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> acknowledging Happ’s struggles against southpaws.</p><p>He entered play Tuesday with a .530 OPS against lefties versus his .820 number against right-handers.</p><p>Newly acquired outfielder <b>Tyrone Taylor</b> started instead. He went 0-for-3 but brought a .301 batting average and a .900 OPS in his 77 previous plate appearances against lefties.</p><p>Counsell didn’t make it sound like a permanent banishment for Happ, one of the mainstays of the Cubs’ lineup.</p><p>‘‘Ian’s still going to play against some lefties,’’ Counsell said. ‘‘But Tyrone gives us somebody — he’s going to get at-bats against left-handed pitching, for sure.’’</p><h3>Tough on Tucker</h3><p>Fans let former Cubs outfielder <b>Kyle Tucker</b> know how they felt about his decision to sign a $240 million offseason deal with the Dodgers, booing him at every turn.</p><p>Whether they felt spurned or just booed him for joining the best team in baseball, they let Tucker have it.</p><p>Then Tucker let them have it with a homer in the second inning.</p>

entries.title: Time for Chicago to buy into public-owned grocery store concept
entries.summary: <p>Another seven <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/25/shoppers-left-stranded-as-save-a-lot-grocery-stores-permanently-close-we-have-to-eat-too" >grocery stores closed</a> on Chicago’s South and West sides last month, leaving thousands of families wondering where they’ll buy fresh food next.</p><p>More closures are another reminder that access to something as basic as groceries remains fragile, depending on your ZIP code.</p><p>Unfortunately, we’ve seen this movie before.</p><p>In 2023, the city of Chicago approved <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2025/10/20/save-a-lot-yellow-banana-city-deal-grocery-requirements-penalties" >roughly $26 million in incentives</a> to help Yellow Banana renovate and reopen Save A Lot stores, including $13.5 million in taxpayer financing. Now seven of those stores are shuttered.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7c0000" name="module-7c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>More than a decade ago, city and federal leaders invested roughly $20 million to bring a Whole Foods to Englewood, heralding it as proof that private investment could solve decades of food disinvestment. When that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2022/5/2/23054290/lightfoot-whole-foods-closing-englewood-prices-replacement-store-emanuel" >Whole Foods closed</a>, the community was left right back where it started.</p><p>Governmental bodies keep writing the same checks and expecting a different <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/5/9/23063658/food-deserts-englewood-whole-foods-public-option-for-groceries-ameya-pawar-paul-williams-other-views" target="_blank" >ending</a>.</p><p>Grocery stores are a business. And no private investor would put millions of dollars into a business only to receive no ownership stake, no collateral and no accountability — then simply hope everything works out. Yet, that’s effectively how politicians have approached grocery access for decades. Taxpayer dollars help finance private operators, but when those operators decide the business no longer works, they leave. The public loses its investment, neighborhoods lose their grocery store and residents once again pay the price.</p><p>There is a better way.</p><p>Instead of repeatedly subsidizing private companies without long-term protections, the city should establish a public grocery option.</p><p>That doesn’t mean replacing every private grocery store. It means recognizing that in neighborhoods where the market has repeatedly failed, grocery access should be treated like any other essential public service. We don’t rely solely on the private market to decide where libraries, parks, schools or fire stations belong. Access to healthy, affordable food deserves the same level of public commitment.</p><p>The good news is Chicago doesn’t have to start from scratch.</p><p>Economic Security Project’s work on this issue, particularly with the funding of a feasibility study, concluded that public grocery stores in Chicago are <a class="Link" href="https://economicsecurityproject.org/resource/opening-the-door-to-public-grocery-stores/" target="_blank" >necessary, feasible and implementable</a>. More importantly, that research from the nonprofit helped spark a national conversation.</p><p>Other cities are already acting on ideas that originated here.</p><p>Atlanta is preparing to open its <a class="Link" href="https://atlanta.urbanize.city/post/azalea-fresh-downtown-market-success-2nd-location-coming" target="_blank" >second city-backed Azalea Fresh Market</a> after the first served more than 150,000 customers while offering prices 18% to 22% below comparable grocery stores. New York City recently <a class="Link" href="https://abc7ny.com/post/city-owned-groceries-offer-30-discounts-essential-items-mamdani-vows-not-compete-local-shops/19584926/" target="_blank" >announced plans to open five publicly owned grocery stores by 2029</a>, targeting neighborhoods with limited food access while aiming to offer staple items at discounts of up to 30%.</p><p>Meanwhile, Chicago — the city that helped prove the concept — is still watching another subsidized grocery chain walk away.</p><p>Public grocery stores don’t have to operate in isolation. Chicago has an extraordinary network of neighborhood food pantries, urban farms, food co-ops and nonprofit organizations already addressing food insecurity every day, so the city is already coordinating around a publicly owned market. A public grocery network could partner with those organizations, strengthen local supply chains, support local producers and create a more resilient food system, rather than forcing community organizations to scramble every time another private operator closes its doors.</p><p>Today, Chicago has seven vacant grocery stores that are already built out for food retail. The infrastructure exists. The research exists. The technical expertise exists. What’s missing is the willingness to stop repeating failed strategies.</p><p>Every grocery closure is treated like an isolated event requiring another emergency subsidy package to attract the next operator. But after years of watching stores open with public assistance only to close a few years later, it’s clear new solutions are needed.</p><p>Chicago has an opportunity to lead again. There is still time to rethink how the city combats food deserts by using these vacant locations to pilot a public grocery network. Instead of simply hoping another private chain succeeds where others have failed, the city can build an institution designed to serve neighborhoods for the long haul.</p><p>The question isn’t whether Chicago can afford to try something different.</p><p>After millions of public dollars have produced empty storefront after empty storefront, the better question is whether we can afford not to.</p><p><i>Erion Malasi is the Illinois director of policy and research at Economic Security Project and a national expert on public option grocery stores.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-000000" name="module-000000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: To Share or Not To Share the Family Secrets?
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> There are two significant secrets in my family, and as I'm a member of the oldest generation and likely in my last decade, I wonder if they should see the light of day.</p><p>The first involves my cousin. He's a year older than I am and doesn't know he was adopted. My older sister was 10 when his parents brought him home. She remembers it vividly, and my mother and I talked about it from time to time. My cousin has led a challenged life of addiction and estrangement. He blames his parents and "inherited characteristics" for many of his problems — his mother's addiction to anxiety meds, his father's poor eyesight, etc. Should I share with him what I know?</p><p>The second secret involves my first wife. We divorced 40 years ago, and although we don't talk, our two children are a prominent part of my life. My ex lives a life of isolation. She is angry and has difficult relations with everyone. What I know is that she had a baby while in high school and gave it up for adoption. I suspect that her guilt about it has caused her withdrawal and alienation from everyone in her family. Should I share with our children that they have an older half-sibling? — <i>KEEPER OF SECRETS</i></p><p><b>DEAR KEEPER:</b> I think the answers to your questions are yes and no. I do think it might help your cousin if you told him the truth about his adoption, in case he might like to contact any living birth relatives to get an accurate family history or medical history.</p><p>However, as far as revealing your first wife's secret, I don't think it would be wise, kind or helpful to out her to your children. She was a minor at the time, and her parents may have been responsible for what happened to her child. Rather than being consumed with guilt or shame, she may still be mourning the loss of that baby.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My parents had three kids. The oldest is married with five kids. The second is married with two kids. The third is single, has mild autism and has trouble meeting people. Our parents don't seem too concerned about the youngest being perpetually single, but he is unable to live on his own due to credit card debt that he can't pay back. He doesn't want to live with anyone unless he finds a romantic partner. What happens if he ends up being single for life? Is there anything that anybody can do to help him before our parents die? — <i>FACING THE FUTURE</i></p><p><b>DEAR FACING THE FUTURE:</b> Has this sibling considered declaring bankruptcy? Mild autism should not stop him from living on his own again once his financial situation improves. A financial adviser or credit counselor may be able to help him with that. The National Foundation for Credit Counseling (nfcc.org) is a good place to start.</p><p>Encourage your brother to join social groups that suit his hobbies and interests. If a club has in-person meetups in a quiet space, he may be able to attend comfortably without becoming overstimulated. He may not find romance, but he could make new friends, easing everyone's anxiety about his future.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p>

entries.title: Helping clear the air with electric buses
entries.summary: <p>Three weeks ago, the Chicago area endured the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/16/wildfire-smoke-air-quality-kn95-mask-sales" >worst air quality levels</a> ever recorded. But it's wrong to think the air is now safe and our health isn't in danger. Our region has a chronic air pollution problem because we create and breathe dangerous levels of toxic diesel tailpipe pollution all year long.</p><p>Chicago is uniquely situated as a major transportation hub. We have <a class="Link" href="https://elpc.org/blog/cut-diesel-pollution-while-maintaining-chicagos-robust-freight-business/" target="_blank" >more diesel trains and trucks</a> entering and exiting our area than anywhere between the East and West coasts, generating dangerous air pollution. As a result,<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/04/22/chicago-area-air-quality-american-lung-association-earth-day-annual-report" > Chicago consistently ranks high</a> on the list of cities globally with the worst air quality. And with summer smog season now in full swing, we can expect to experience more days where the outside air is unsafe to breathe, especially for children, seniors and people with chronic lung conditions. </p><p>But there are glimmers of hope. At the end of March, the Chicago Transit Authority issued a <a class="Link" href="https://www.highergov.com/sl/contract-opportunity/il-c26fi103254072-request-for-proposals-r-67069630/" target="_blank" >request for proposal</a> seeking bids to acquire at least 30 clean battery-electric transit buses. This is the next step in the CTA’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/2/22/22945636/cta-electric-bus-fleet-phase-in-2040" >“Charging Forward” plan</a>, which aims for the full electrification of agency's bus fleet by 2040. Right now, there are <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/02/07/electric-bus-cta-pace-illinois-epa-pritzker" target="_blank" >25 electric buses</a> in the CTA’s fleet of roughly 2,000 buses. Acquiring more electric CTA buses will eliminate the choking pollution passengers and pedestrians would otherwise inhale and helps protect those with chronic health conditions.</p><p>Also promising is the "Project Zero" plan Pace has in place. The goal: electrify its 733-bus fleet by 2040. The agency currently has 47 hybrid-electric buses and at least one electric bus service. There are also plans for an additional 22 electric fixed route buses this year. </p><p>Before the 2040 target date approaches to convert all CTA and Pace buses to electric, let's continue to support initiatives to reduce air pollution in our city and suburbs to protect the most vulnerable residents.</p><p><i>Brian Urbaszewski,</i><b><i> </i></b><i>director, Environmental Health Programs, Respiratory Health Association</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-790000" name="module-790000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Op-ed strengthened my determination </h3><p>As I finished reading Saturday's Sun-Times, I was overwhelmed by a strong sense of crisis. I first read Lisa Kurian Philip's well-reported article about faculty and staff layoffs at my alma mater, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/07/31/illinois-institute-of-technology-cuts-160-faculty-and-staff-just-before-fall-semester" >Illinois Institute of Technology</a>. Suddenly, the federal government policies and attitudes toward international students at schools hit closer to home. A few weeks ago, three fellow alums and I met for our annual lunch or dinner visit. We have gathered every year since 1966. Illinois Tech is the place where the borders of my world were stretched and where my eyes were opened to diversities I had not previously experienced. I left with a degree in my hand and new people in my heart.</p><p>With the feelings attached to those memories, I then read David McGrath’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/07/31/president-donald-trump-cold-blooded-leader-death-iran-ice-shootings-covid-measles-david-mcgrath" >op-ed</a> on the current reality in our country. His piece headlined "Trump is our cold-blooded leader" summarized the tragedy of the current experiences we are living through. Different articles or sound bites or news summaries can lessen the impact of events. McGrath gave me a wide-angle lens to see the scope of what is happening to us. He summarizes the details and exposes the immorality. He strengthened my resolve to not be guilty of “saying nothing” while it happens.</p><p>Thank you, David</p><p><i>The Rev. Bill Stenzel, Cedar Lake, Indiana</i></p><h3>Tin man Trump </h3><p>David McGrath's piece, "Our cold-blooded leader," helped confirm what I have long thought. I notice when the national anthem is being sung and at other solemn events, while others have their hands over their hearts, Donald Trump salutes. Maybe I'm right; no heart.</p><p><i>Lenore Bernstein, Northbrook</i></p><h3>We all pay with healthcare cuts </h3><p>The recent Sun-Times article on the dramatic increase in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/07/31/cook-county-predicts-charity-care-will-soar-to-highest-level-in-more-than-a-decade-medicaid-obamacare" >uncompensated care</a> at the Cook County Health system is a graphic reminder that cuts in healthcare support don’t actually save much money — they just redistribute costs.</p><p>When people lose health coverage, some will feel forced to forego healthcare. But many will still need healthcare, and in many cases, more expensive care than if they had earlier access to care. Just because Medicaid or Affordable Care Act support went away, the real costs to provide this healthcare don’t go away. This forces doctors and hospitals to raise their rates for the rest of us, which leads to higher insurance costs and more out-of-pocket costs.</p><p>In short, the actual impact of reducing health supports is increased pain among those directly impacted and increased costs for the rest of us. Since the benefits of the Republican budget bill went disproportionately the most wealthy, cuts in healthcare support shift money from most citizens to the wealthy, while increasing suffering.</p><p>Is this the society we want?</p><p><i>Mike Koetting, Fulton River District</i></p><h3>Don’t forget what Tunney did</h3><p>Every <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/restaurants/2026/08/03/ann-sather-stellas-diner" >article</a> about former 44th Ward Ald. Tom Tunney and his restaurants should include the fact that he had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2020/12/7/22158783/indoor-dining-restrictions-tom-tunney-ann-sather-restaurant-covid-19" >allowed indoor dining</a> during the height of a pandemic that killed over 1 million Americans. That should be an albatross around his neck.</p><p><i>Ben Snow, Edgewater</i> </p><h3>Mass shootings are the norm </h3><p>While many patrons went into the Twin Falls, Idaho, In-N-Out Burger Saturday, not <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/bystander-handgun-distracted-gunman-fatal-shooting-rcna590473" target="_blank" >everyone came out alive</a>. Yeah, it was another mass shooting in the land of the free and the home of legalized murder. Of course, the incident made the newspapers — just not the front page in most places. After all, there's that senseless war still raging in the Middle East and the price of beef is approaching <a class="Link" href="https://www.syracuse.com/data/2026/06/beef-prices-surge-close-to-7-a-pound-in-latest-data-syracusecom-grocery-price-tracker.html" target="_blank" >$7 a pound</a>. Seemingly unnoticed is the indisputable fact that human life is now grossly undervalued while a fill-up at the gas station is overpriced and rising.</p><p><i>Bob Ory, Elgin</i><br></p>

entries.title: People have been fermenting food for millennia. Here's why more people are focused on gut health now
entries.summary: <p>More people are focusing on their gut health, as fibermaxxing goes mainstream, colorectal cancer rises among young adults and personalized gut microbiome treatments become increasingly popular.</p><p>Now, a generation- and culture-spanning way of preserving food is in the spotlight: fermentation. <b></b> The federal government's latest dietary guidelines specifically encourage Americans to eat more fermented food.</p><p>The foods have been further popularized by followers of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s Make America Healthy Again movement. And while other diet fads championed by MAHA have been questioned by health experts — like unproven claims about raw milk and seed oils — there's some science behind the benefits of eating fermented foods. <b></b><b></b></p><p>Fermented foods go back thousands of years , to the days when we needed to keep food from spoiling but didn't have refrigerators. Many cultures have traditional fermented foods: yogurt, kimchi, sauerkraut, South Indian idli and dosa.</p><p>Dietitians and doctors say they're a great addition to almost anyone's diet, but they warn against new, mass-produced products.</p><p>Here's what to know.</p><h3>Not all fermented foods are made equal</h3><p>Fermentation is a process by which naturally occurring microbes including bacteria and yeast break down and preserve food.</p><p>The foods are a hot research topic, though many of their health benefits are already clear, experts say.</p><p>"We've been doing this for ages and we just found out more recently that it's actually helped our gut health," said Dr. Lisa Ganjhu, a gastroenterologist with New York University Langone Health.</p><p>Still, it doesn't automatically mean something is healthy if it's fermented.</p><p>"Beer and wine are fermented foods, but they're not necessarily probiotics," she said. "If anything, they influence our own microbiome in more of a negative way."</p><p>Barbara Olendzki, director the University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School's Center for Applied Nutrition, said she recommends people focus on "whole fermented foods" like fermented beets or green beans in addition to foods like yogurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut and tempeh.</p><h3>Fermented foods feed the gut in two main ways</h3><p>The microbes in fermented foods help predigest it, breaking it down and changing the compounds available in it. The bacteria themselves also help keep the gut in balance, by competing with other bacteria — some of them less beneficial — already in your intestines.</p><p>Some fermented foods, like yogurt, give you the live probiotics while you're eating them. Others, like sourdough bread, give you few, if any, because they've been baked or otherwise processed in ways that kill the microbes. But there's evidence that some fermented foods are beneficial even without the live microbes, Dalia Perelman, a Stanford University research dietitian, said.</p><h3>Beware of marketing hype</h3><p>Experts warn against sodas, chocolate or other processed foods that market themselves as probiotic. Even probiotic supplements are essentially trying to replicate the combinations of beneficial bacteria that naturally grow in many fermented foods, Perelman said.</p><p>"Consumers are getting excited about it and trying to choose products that are fermented and with the idea that it's very 'gut healthy,' which is not a clinical definition," she said. "And then the marketing is running with this trend."</p><p>Avoid sugary items, too, Ganjhu said. Extra sugar feeds negative bacteria as opposed to the positive bacteria in fermented foods, she said.</p><p>And look for items that say "live cultures," not just that they're probiotic.</p><p>"The best yogurt you can have is just plain, fermented milk with culture," she said. "Let it do its business."</p><h3>Can fermented foods be risky?</h3><p><b></b> While the category of fermented foods is broad, experts say they're generally safe for most people. And not just for health reasons — they also add interesting and diverse flavors to your plate. <b></b></p><p>Perelman said people who have weakened immune systems and those with irritable bowl disease may want to talk to their doctors before incorporating the foods into their diet. Some people could experience different reactions depending on which type of fermented food they're eating.</p><p>Olendzki said some people might experience bloating, gas and other discomfort when introducing more fermented foods, especially as their gut adjusts.</p><p>"If you feel good, keep drinking it. You don't feel good? Stop," Ganjhu said. She noted that the same foods affect people differently.</p><h3>Eat a diverse mix of fermented foods consistently</h3><p><b>ck for print</b> So which fermented food is the best? You'll be hard-pressed to find a scientifically backed ranking that puts sauerkraut over kimchi, or tells you to eat a bowl of yogurt and call it a day. <b></b></p><p>The best way to eat fermented foods is to eat lots of different kinds, and to make them a regular part of your diet, experts say.</p><p>Ganjhu recommended thinking about the foods in categories, like milk-based yogurt and kefir, and fiber-based ones such as kimchi and sauerkraut.</p><p>Researchers are also still exploring if it matters how much fermented foods people eat. Just like so many things with diet, the answer is likely very different person to person, experts said.</p><p>"We can hedge our bets and just get a variety," Perelman said. She suggested aiming for two servings a day.</p><p>And the foods should be one part of a well-rounded diet, so the good bacteria you're introducing to your gut have things they like to eat, like fibrous prebiotics. They feed the probiotics, which are the live bacteria themselves.</p><p>"Just go slow and drink a lot of water. It also matters what the rest of the diet looks like," Olendzki said. "It's not just one thing."</p><p><i>The Associated Press Health and Science Department receives support from the Howard Hughes Medical Institute's Department of Science Education and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. The AP is solely responsible for all content.</i></p>

entries.title: Despite disinvestment, a longtime West Sider has stayed put with the help of block clubs
entries.summary: <p>Helen King sits in her dining room in Chicago’s West Garfield Park neighborhood. She’s been living in the home for more than 50 years and chuckles at the couch and lampshades covered in plastic.</p><p>“Can you imagine that color if I didn’t have plastic on? All the kids and stuff,” she said.</p><p>King raised her children here with her late husband Harry. She takes pride that her couches are still their original shade of yellow.</p><p>“Alexa, play Ray Charles,” she said as she walked over to the kitchen.</p><p>The music takes her back to summer parties organized by her block club. Neighbors gathered outside for some barbecue and good company.</p><p>“We all needed and wanted the same things,” King said of her block club. “We wanted success, and we wanted our kids to be safe.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-180000" name="image-180000"></a> <picture </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Chicago Sun-Times/ST-13003366-0016, Chicago History Museum</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Today, you’ll still see evidence of block clubs in South and West Side neighborhoods: colorful signs, often wooden and hand-painted. They might be decorated with flowers and trees, and most tell readers what is allowed or not allowed on the block.</p><p>Block clubs are coalitions of neighbors who volunteer to improve the physical and social conditions of their block. That can range from planting flowers on the parkway to buying abandoned homes in order to increase the neighborhood’s market value. These clubs differ from homeowners associations because they are not legally mandated for residents to participate in or pay fees toward.</p><p>The history of block clubs in Chicago go back to the Great Migration. According to Amanda Seligman, author of “Chicago’s Block Clubs: How Neighbors Shape the City,” block clubs likely originated in Atlanta. In 1908, Lugenia Burns Hope started the Atlanta Neighborhood Union, where she and a team of mothers worked to bring education and health programs to African American families. It’s often credited as the roadmap for the Civil Rights movements and block clubs.</p><p>“[Block clubs] really grew to their mature form in Chicago, especially thanks to the work of the Chicago Urban League,” said Seligman, who is a professor of history and urban studies at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee.</p><p>During the early 20th century, over 6 million African Americans left the Jim Crow South for Northern cities like Chicago, Detroit and New York. The Chicago Urban League helped to provide financial and community support, including the formation of block clubs.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Curious City sat down with King to learn how her block has changed throughout the decades.</p><h3><b>Why Mrs. King stays </b></h3><p>Helen King is a member of the Westside Block Club Association. When the association leader, Talei Thompson, started the block club, he was told to speak with neighbors and elders like King. She moved to Chicago in the 1950s from Jackson, Mississippi, when she was 19 with her sister and two brothers.</p><p><i>This conversation has been condensed and edited for clarity. </i></p><p><b>After you moved to Chicago, what happened? </b></p><p> I did get a job, and I kept a job until I eventually retired. I got  married, and my husband and I was able to purchase our own home, something that we picked out, and I’m so pleased with it.</p><p><b>What were block clubs like when you first bought your home?</b></p><p>[Neighbors] come and knock on your door. We’d meet at each other’s home, once a month. We’d have little refreshments, and if we had issues or if we were planning anything, we would just discuss stuff that was important.</p><p>I kept track of the funds we took up, and [information] of the [city] offices [as secretary].</p><p>It starts with a small group and then it grows. Back in the day, we’d take the kids on trips and we’d have cookouts for the kids. We didn’t do an awful lot because we paid very little, $5 or something, nothing much. But it was just the idea that everybody owned their own home, so they wanted something.</p><p>If one had a problem, then the next had a problem. We worked together. We all needed and wanted the same things. Now we don’t have one movie [theater].</p><p>We had recreational facilities for teenagers. I used to take my boys to youth classes for the kids to play and jump and do whatever they wanted to do. We don’t even have a grocery store in the neighborhood [now].</p><p>Back in the day, we had really good city workers, like garbage pickup. It was pleasant, it was different.</p><p><b>What do you think is behind these challenges on the block today? </b></p><p> It’s a lot of absentee landlords over here now. I doubt if I know three landlords over here.
